The last post ended with a promise: graphical causal models next. That was May 2025. I still owe you that post, and it is coming.

What happened in between is that my work moved into official statistics, and I have spent most of that time around one strange, enormous exercise: the census. Before that I thought of the census the way most people do. Somebody comes to the door once every ten years, asks a few questions, and a big number appears in the newspaper a year later.

I was wrong about how much hangs on that number. So before I write anything technical about it, I want to start from zero.

If you live in India, this is a good year to start from zero. The country is in the middle of its first census since 2011. The first phase, where every house is listed, [was scheduled between April and September this year](https://www.deccanherald.com/india/houselisting-first-phase-of-census-2027-to-take-place-between-april-september-ministry-of-home-affairs-3854508), and the head count itself follows in February 2027. It is the first one done digitally, with [around 3 million people](https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/odisha-govt-plans-april-start-for-census-2027-houselisting-exercise-126010801121_1.html) deployed for the first phase alone.

Three million people, sent out to ask questions. Why would any country do that?

To answer that I need to back up one step, because the census is the biggest piece of something larger that most of us never think about.

## What are official statistics?

::: {.box .box-key}

***Official statistics are the numbers a state produces about itself, as a public good, under rules that are supposed to keep them honest.***

:::

You already use them every day without calling them that. The inflation rate that decides your fixed deposit is worth less this year. The unemployment rate that gets quoted in every election debate. Literacy rate, sex ratio, GDP growth, the poverty line. None of these fall from the sky. An office somewhere collected the data, cleaned it, and published it.

What makes a number *official* is not that the government likes it. Often it is the opposite. The United Nations has ten [Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics](https://unstats.un.org/fpos), adopted by its Statistical Commission in 1994 and endorsed by the General Assembly in 2014. Read them once, they fit on two pages. The ones I keep coming back to:

- The numbers are for everyone. The very first principle says official statistics serve the government, the economy **and the public**, and that citizens are entitled to them.
- Methods are chosen on professional grounds, and published, so anyone can check how a number was made.
- What you tell the statistics office about yourself stays confidential and is used for statistics only.

Remember that last one. It will show up again.

## So what is a census?

Of everything a statistics office produces, the census is the oldest and the largest. The word comes from the Latin *censere*, to assess. The Romans counted citizens to know whom to tax and whom to send to war. Not the most charming origin story, I know.

The modern idea is kinder, and more precise. The UN's [Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses](https://unstats.un.org/UNSDWebsite/statcom/session_56/documents/BG-3b-Draft_P&R_4th_Rev-E.pdf) lists the features that make a count a census. In plain words:

::: {.box}

1. **Every person is recorded separately.** Not "about 40 people live in this lane", but each one, with their own age, sex, education, work.
2. **Everyone in the territory is covered.** No sampling of who gets counted.
3. **Everyone is counted as of the same moment.** For most of India that moment is 1 March 2027. Born on 2 March? You are in the next one.
4. **It repeats at a fixed interval,** usually ten years, so you can compare.
5. **It can give numbers for small areas.** Your district, your town, your ward.

:::

Number 5 is the one people underestimate, and it is easiest to see next to a survey. A survey can tell you the unemployment rate of a state, because a few thousand well-chosen households are enough for that. It cannot tell you how many children under six live in your block, because it probably did not visit your block at all. Only something that covers everyone can.

And here is the part that took me a while to appreciate: surveys need the census too. To choose a few thousand households "well", you need a list of all the households to choose from, and you need to know what the whole population looks like so that you can check your sample against it. That list and that picture come from the census. Every survey you have ever read about is standing on one.

## Fine. But why should I care?

That explains why statisticians care about the census. You should care for a different reason: the count is used to divide things up, and three of them are close to home.

### 1. Your food

India's National Food Security Act says subsidised grain should reach about two-thirds of the population. Two-thirds of *which* population? The law points to the latest published census, and for more than a decade that has meant 2011.

The country did not stop growing in 2011. The quota did. In 2020 the economists Jean Drèze, Reetika Khera and Meghana Mungikar [estimated](https://www.indiaspend.com/more-than-100mn-excluded-from-pds-as-govt-uses-outdated-census-2011-data) that more than 100 million people who should have been covered were left out for this one reason. By 2025 Drèze put the figure [above 120 million](https://m.thewire.in/article/economy/census-delays-leave-120-million-indians-without-access-to-foodgrain). These are estimates built on population projections, and you can argue with the projections. But the mechanism is not in dispute: no new count, no new quota.

Nobody decided to exclude those people. An old number did it quietly.

### 2. Your vote

Food is not the only thing running on an old count. Parliament is too. How many seats does your state get in the Lok Sabha? The answer is still based on the **1971** census. The allocation was frozen in 1976 and the freeze was later extended until the first census after 2026. Which is the one happening now.

This is why the census has been in the political news all year. In April 2026 a constitutional amendment that would have redrawn seats using 2011 figures [failed in the Lok Sabha](https://www.livelaw.in/amp/top-stories/lok-sabha-rejects-constitution-131st-bill-2026-on-delimitation-530736). The one-third reservation for women passed in 2023 is also tied to a redrawing of seats that waits on a census. Whatever your view on how seats should be shared between states, and people hold strong views on this, the argument is about what to do with a count.

Does it matter how many people share one MP? There is some evidence that it does. A [study of Indian constituencies](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0259150) by Rikhil Bhavnani found that a 10% increase in representation led to a 0.6% increase in night-time lights, a common stand-in for economic activity. A small effect, but a measurable one.

### 3. Your state's money

Seats are one thing a count divides. Money is the other, and the clearest numbers on that come from the United States, where the Census Bureau [worked out](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2023/decennial-census-federal-funds-distribution.html) that 353 federal programmes used its data to distribute more than $2.8 trillion in a single year, 2021. Schools, hospitals, roads, school lunches.

Now a caution, because this is where census advocacy tends to oversell. A big total does not mean each uncounted person costs their town a fortune. Michael Murray [ran the numbers](https://doi.org/10.2307/2061820) for the 1990 US census and found that correcting the undercount would have moved about $56 per miscounted person, far less than people assumed. The pot is fixed, so one place's gain is another's loss, and most formulas use other things besides population.

So the right way to say it is: the count does not create money. It decides who gets which slice.

Food, seats and money are the visible uses. Under all three sits something simpler. Every rate you have ever seen is one number divided by another. Deaths per 1,000 people. Doctors per 100,000. Vaccinated children out of all children. The top number comes from hospitals and clinics. The bottom number, the *denominator*, comes from the census or from projections based on it. Andrew Tatem's [review after Covid-19](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epidem.2022.100641) makes the point that the pandemic exposed how old and shaky those local population numbers were in many countries. If the denominator is wrong, every rate built on it is wrong, and you will not see it by looking at the rate.

## Not all censuses knock on doors

With this much riding on the count, you would expect every country to do it the same careful way, door by door. They do not, and this surprised me the most when I started: there is more than one way to count a country.

| Flavour | How the counting is done | Examples |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Traditional | Every household fills in a questionnaire, with an enumerator, on paper or online | India, United States |
| Register-based | Nobody is asked anything. The count is assembled from records the state already holds | Denmark, Finland, Sweden |
| Combined | Registers for the basics, plus a questionnaire or survey for what the registers lack | Estonia, Liechtenstein |
| Rolling | A different part of the country is surveyed each year, averaged over a cycle | France |

: Four ways to run a census

The direction of travel is clear. Among the countries of the UN's European region, traditional censuses [fell from 32 to 24](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic-social/meetings/2023/egm-20231213/docs/s03-01-ECE.pdf) between the 2010 and 2020 rounds, and only 6 said they expect to run one in 2030. Cost is a big part of it. In the 2010 round the median traditional census cost [$5.57 per person; a fully register-based one cost $0.24](https://census.gov/content/dam/Census/programs-surveys/international-programs/stic/using_administrative_data.pdf).

Twenty-three times cheaper, and no door-knocking. Sounds like a free lunch, right? It is not, but that is a story for the next post.

## When the count goes wrong, or does not happen

Whichever flavour a country picks, the count will have errors in it. A census is never perfect, and the good offices measure their own mistakes. After the 2020 US census, a follow-up survey found the total was nearly right, but the errors were not spread evenly. [Hispanic residents were undercounted by about 5%, Black residents by 3.3%, Native Americans on reservations by 5.6%](https://csmonitor.com/USA/2022/0311/2020-census-undercounts-Black-Hispanic-Native-American-residents), while non-Hispanic white residents were overcounted. The people who are hardest to count are usually the people who most need to be counted. It is the same in every country I have read about.

Then there is the case where the count becomes a prize. Nigeria's [last census was in 2006](https://allafrica.com/stories/202606300083.html), twenty years ago. Demographers Oka Obono and Elizabeth Omoluabi [explain why it is so hard there](https://doi.org/10.11564/27-2-472): population decides revenue shares and political representation, so every region has a reason to want a bigger number, and every result gets contested.

Nigeria is not alone. UNFPA [reports](https://www.unfpa.org/census) that 35 countries did not hold a census at all in the 2020 round. That is about 2.4 billion people living in places governed with numbers from another decade.

## "But we have so much data now"

At this point a fair question is whether we still need any of this. In my first post I wrote that the world generates petabytes of data every minute. So why send 3 million people door to door?

Because almost none of that data covers *everyone*. A phone company knows where its SIM cards are. A bank knows its account holders. A satellite can see roofs. Each one misses somebody, and it is not random who gets missed.

Researchers have got very good at estimating population from satellite images in places with no recent count. I have built one of these models myself, for a country in the Middle East: a Bayesian hierarchical model that predicts population from night-time lights and vegetation indices. I find the work fascinating. But notice what I needed to build it. The model had to learn from real census counts before it could predict anything. The [people who develop these methods](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1715305115) say the same thing: they complement a national count and do not replace it. Without something solid underneath, a clever estimate has nothing to be checked against.

## One uncomfortable thing

A count that covers everyone is also a list of everyone. Remember the confidentiality principle from the start of this post? It exists because it has been broken.

The historians Margo Anderson and William Seltzer have [documented](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-38619-0) how US census data was used in the incarceration of Japanese Americans during the Second World War. That is the worst-case answer to "what could go wrong if the state knows where everyone is".

I do not think this is a reason to refuse the census. I think it is a reason to care about how it is run: who can see individual records, what the law says, and whether the statistics office can say no to the rest of the government. A citizen who knows what a census is can ask those questions. One who thinks it is a form to get rid of cannot.

So when the enumerator comes in February, answer properly. And when the results come out, go and look up your own district. It is your data, quite literally.

Next time: how do you count a country without knocking on a single door?
